description: Extras talks from BSides Las Vegas 2021.

talks.title: Lockpicking intro
talks.teaser: Shows the internal parts of a pin tumbler lock and explains how picking sets each pin.
talks.summary:
This short interstitial clip introduces lockpicking by showing the mechanism of a common pin tumbler lock up close. It describes the two stacks of pins in the cylinder: driver pins that are all the same length, and key pins cut to different heights that give each key its unique profile. A clear demonstration padlock makes the plug, the shear line between the plug and the housing, and the retaining pin easy to see.

The core idea is that picking replaces a key one pin at a time instead of all at once. Each driver pin has to be lifted until it sits at the shear line, which frees the plug to turn. Once every pin is set, the plug rotates, a latch releases, and the spring-loaded shackle pops open. The presenter notes that this cheap lock opens quickly and that most locks a beginner will encounter use this same mechanism, differing mainly in the number of pins.

The clip closes with guidance on feel. Holding light tension on the plug makes set pins noticeable, because they stop springing back, so the picker can tell which pins have been lifted and must keep that tension until all of them are in place. The clip ends with a brief sign-off encouraging viewers to practice.

talks.title: tabletop excercise cootie catcher
talks.teaser: Shows how to fold a paper cootie catcher that picks threat actors, attack vectors and business impacts for a tabletop exercise.
talks.summary:
This interstitial from BSidesLV 2021's Camp Stay At Home segment is a playful craft session hosted by a camp counselor character. Its subject is a paper fold-and-write tool, known as a cootie catcher, that can be used to build a tabletop exercise on the spot.

The segment walks through the folding steps. The host creases a square sheet, folds the corners into the center, and then marks the visible panels. The outer flaps are labeled for threat actors, such as an insider, the next layer for attack vectors, such as a misconfiguration, and the eight inner triangles for business impacts, such as the loss of employee personal data. Players choose a value from each layer, open the folds, and read out the resulting scenario.

The host finishes by refolding the paper into its finger-puppet shape, with the threat actors showing on the outside. The takeaway is a low-cost, low-tech way for a group to generate and vary incident response scenarios before running a discussion-based exercise.

talks.title: Campfire Talks
talks.teaser: Gathers storytellers who share short true tales of social engineering, investigations and infrastructure mishaps.
talks.summary:
This is a virtual campfire night of short personal stories recorded at BSides Las Vegas in 2021. A panel of judges asks each storyteller follow-up questions before the next person steps up.

Duncan Sparrow opens with a 1990 cyber operation linked to Operation Desert Shield, covering undercover roles and a plan to interfere with Iraqi air defense communications that arrived too late. Another storyteller describes a months-long intrusion into a network appliance vendor, where attackers reached a PAM module and took source code and signing material, and argues that single sign-on without extra verification was a weak point. Alice Hardy recounts a junior analyst struggling with PowerShell on a server and getting flagged, a lesson about supervision. Ian Meyer tells of slipping into a theme park's service tunnels as a teenager.

Later tales cover a managed provider whose logs and backups vanished after its contract was cancelled, an intern's looped cable that took retail sites offline, and a river that froze enough to walk across during an assessment. The night closes with BSides Las Vegas origin history, and Ian Meyer is named the winner. Practical takeaways include keeping logging on, storing backups off-site, adding checks beyond single sign-on, and planning carefully before cutting a vendor's access.

talks.title: shrub
talks.teaser: Shows how to make a shrub, a fruit, sugar and vinegar drink, as a non-alcoholic option for guests.
talks.summary:
In this short BSides Las Vegas 2021 interstitial, Alan Friedman argues that hosts should have a good non-alcoholic option ready for guests who are not drinking. He describes a shrub as something more satisfying than a plain soft drink, and a practical choice for gatherings.

The method is simple. Pick a juicy fruit with little pulp or small seeds, such as strawberries, melon or peaches, slice it thin and cover it with sugar, roughly a quarter of the fruit's weight. Over a day or two the sugar draws out the juice. The liquid is strained, the fruit is returned briefly to pull out the last of its flavour, and then apple cider vinegar is added to the syrup in an amount adjusted to taste. Fruits like blueberries and figs are a poor fit because their small bits end up in the syrup.

To serve, a few tablespoons of the concentrate go into a glass topped with fizzy water, with a bit of fruit as garnish. The takeaway is that the base is mostly sugar and acid, so it keeps in the fridge for months, and it can also serve as the starting point for a cocktail.

talks.title: M80 in the campfie
talks.teaser: Shows how to smoke a glass with rosemary and build a smoky, campfire-style old fashioned.
talks.summary:
This short interstitial from the BSidesLV 2021 Camp Stay At Home stream has host Alan Freeman making a campfire-inspired cocktail called the M80 in the campfie. The idea is an old fashioned with a smoky character, and he explains that rosemary or other woody material such as wood chips or a cinnamon stick can supply the smoke.

The segment starts with the smoking technique. A heat-proof surface is set up with a fire extinguisher nearby, and a little wet liquid goes into the glass so the smoke has something to cling to. The herb is lit with a torch until it smoulders, then the glass is inverted over it to trap the scent. The drink itself is built in a different glass: bourbon, spicy bitters for a bit of heat, a brown sugar syrup for a toasted marshmallow note, and a small measure of a smoky Islay scotch. It is poured over a large ice cube and garnished with the charred rosemary.

The talk ends with a relaxed sign-off that wishes viewers well and looks forward to sharing drinks in person. The practical takeaway is that a household torch and a glass can add a convincing smoke aroma to a cocktail without special equipment.

talks.title: hello muddler
talks.teaser: Walks through making a light gin cocktail with muddled cucumber and mint, finished with soda water.
talks.summary:
This short interstitial from BSides Las Vegas 2021's stay-at-home camp series has Alan Friedman making a casual gin drink by the lake. The cocktail is built on muddled cucumber and mint, with a small amount of lemon juice and a homemade syrup. He notes that a sturdy wooden spoon can stand in for a muddler, and that a cocktail jigger is handy but not required.

He explains how to balance the drink. The lemon and sweetener are kept modest so the gin still comes through, and he suggests adjusting the amounts to taste. His homemade simple syrup is equal parts sugar and water heated until dissolved, with tea steeped in it for an iced-tea note, and he says it keeps well in the fridge. The ingredients are shaken with ice to chill and dilute the drink, then strained into a glass.

To finish, he tops the glass with soda water to make the cocktail lighter and easier to drink, and mentions champagne as a fancier option. The segment is aimed at viewers who want a simple drink they can make at home, and it closes with a wish for happy camping.
